name: The Phone Tester
oneLiner: Runs the existing Playwright suite against emulated iOS/Android device profiles and, per failure, emits numbered manual-repro steps plus a device-simulator link.
lead: Executes the app's Playwright tests against the `mobile-chrome` (Android) and `mobile-safari` (iOS) projects, ingests a step-level results file to pin the exact step that broke, then rewrites each failure as numbered manual-repro instructions — open simulator, navigate to the app URL, log in, walk the steps, expected vs. actual — with a ready-made simulator link for the device.
chore: Real-device testing is fiddly: source the devices, log in, tap the same steps, and on a break, hand-write what you did so a dev can repeat it. Doing that on both iOS and Android, per test, with clear repro notes each time, burns hours.
instead: A pass/fail scoreboard per device profile and, per failure, a numbered repro recipe — device, browser, taps, expected, actual — with a simulator link to reproduce it live.
whyItMatters: An unreproducible failure gets argued about and ignored; a failure with numbered steps and a device link gets fixed.

howItWorks.step: Builds and runs the `playwright test` invocation against the selected device project(s) — `mobile-chrome` for Android, `mobile-safari` for iOS, both by default — optionally scoped to one test file, capturing stdout.
howItWorks.explain: Assembles the `playwright test` argv incrementally. The device filter maps `android` → `--project=mobile-chrome` (Pixel on Chromium) and `ios` → `--project=mobile-safari` (iPhone on **WebKit**, so failures reflect the real Safari engine, not Chromium pretending); `all` pushes **no** `--project` flag at all, which is what makes Playwright run every project in the config. An optional `testFile` narrows the run to one spec for chasing a single failure, and `--headed` surfaces the emulated browser. It runs through `execSync` **capturing** stdout — not `stdio: inherit` — because the returned output is parsed afterward, complementing the step-level JSON the reporter writes.

howItWorks.step: Reads back the step-level results — every step's name, duration, and passed/failed/skipped status — from the JSON a separate reporter wrote during the run.
howItWorks.explain: Prefers `step-results-latest.json` — a stable pointer the mobile-step-reporter overwrites every run — and only if it's absent falls back to enumerating `step-results-*.json`, sorting by filename and **reversing** to pick the newest (the timestamped names sort lexically, so reverse = most recent). The reporter writes these **during** the run, not after, which is deliberate: Playwright's own exit doesn't carry step-level detail, so the failing step would be lost otherwise. If neither the latest file nor any timestamped file exists, it throws with a message pointing straight at the likely cause — the reporter wasn't wired in — rather than returning an empty summary that would mask the failure.

howItWorks.step: Maps each tested device to its deep link on the chosen simulator provider, falling back to the provider's base URL if no device-specific link exists.
howItWorks.explain: Resolves a launch URL for each device the run actually exercised — iterating `summary.devices`, not a static list, so only tested devices get links. For each it prefers the provider's **device-specific deep link** from `config.baseUrls[device]`, and the `||` fallback to `https://<provider>.com` handles the case where the provider config has no entry for that device: the reviewer still gets a working link, just to the provider's home rather than straight to the emulator. The returned `device → url` map is what the report writer stitches into each failure's repro steps.

howItWorks.step: Writes the report — a pass/fail table per device and, per failure, numbered manual-repro steps: open the simulator, navigate to the app URL, log in, walk the non-skipped steps, ending in an expected-vs-actual pair.
howItWorks.explain: Turns one failure into a copy-pasteable manual recipe. `browserName` branches on `platform === 'ios'` to say **Safari** vs **Chrome** — matching the engine the emulated device actually runs, so the tester reproduces on the same rendering path that failed. Steps 1-3 are fixed setup (open simulator, navigate to the app URL, log in) and `manualStepNum` starts at **4** so the recorded test steps continue that numbering seamlessly; **skipped** steps are `continue`d past because they never ran and would mislead a human. If a `failedStep` was pinned, the recipe closes with it as **Expected** and its `error.message` (or a generic `'Step failed'` fallback) as **Actual**, giving a dev the precise assertion that broke.

howItWorks.step: Correlates failures across device profiles and emits a rule-based recommendation per pattern — one-platform-only, both-platforms, or timeouts.
howItWorks.explain: Rule-based triage — no LLM — that reads the failure **distribution** across platforms. A clean run short-circuits immediately with the all-passed line. Otherwise it partitions `failedTests` by platform and emits a recommendation only when failures are **exclusively** one-sided: Android-only points at Chrome/Chromium rendering or the Pixel viewport, iOS-only at Safari/WebKit or the iPhone viewport — the asymmetry is the diagnostic, since a both-platforms failure is deliberately left for the caller to read as a likely app-level bug rather than a platform quirk. A separate, **non-exclusive** pass flags any `timedOut` tests as a possible slow-mobile-response cluster, so a run can surface both a platform note and a timeout note at once.

examples.caption: Menu button opens on Android, fails on iOS
examples.input: Suite run on both profiles; the 'open menu' step fails on `mobile-safari`, passes on `mobile-chrome`.
examples.output: Report flags an iOS-only failure, the exact failed step, an iPhone simulator deep link, numbered repro steps, and a Safari/WebKit-specific recommendation.

examples.caption: Feature breaks on both profiles
examples.input: The 'submit form' step fails on both `mobile-chrome` and `mobile-safari`.
examples.output: Marked failing on both devices; recommendation treats it as an app-level bug rather than a platform quirk and prioritizes the fix.

examples.caption: Clean run
examples.input: Full suite passes on both profiles.
examples.output: 100% pass scoreboard and the single all-passed recommendation confirming both Android and iOS profiles are green.

underHood.heading: Running the suite on both device profiles
underHood.input: A device filter (android / ios / all) and an optional single test-file path.
underHood.output: A live Playwright run against the `mobile-chrome` and/or `mobile-safari` projects.

underHood.heading: Ingesting step-level results
underHood.input: The `step-results-*.json` written by the step-level reporter during the run.
underHood.output: A per-test breakdown: each step's name, duration, pass/fail/skipped status, and the first failing step.

underHood.heading: Resolving simulator deep links
underHood.output: A per-device deep link on the configured provider (BrowserStack, LambdaTest, or Appetize).

underHood.heading: Writing the reports
underHood.whenRuns: After results and links are assembled.
underHood.input: The pass/fail scoreboard, the failure list, and the simulator links.
underHood.output: A JSON file, a Markdown report, and — with `--word` — a `.docx`, each with numbered manual-repro steps under every failure.

underHood.heading: Rule-based recommendations
underHood.input: The full failed-test list across both profiles.
underHood.output: Pattern-matched advice — iOS-only, both-platforms (likely app bug), or timeout cluster.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
The target app running at a reachable URL (dev or QA).
An existing Playwright test suite — this agent runs those tests against mobile device profiles, it doesn't author new ones.
~10 min on first run: `npx playwright install` downloads the Chromium and WebKit engines before anything runs.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed by Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: Only needed once per new machine.

steps.label: Install dependencies — once for the agent, once for the Playwright package it drives.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

cd Playwright
npm install
npx playwright install   # downloads the actual Chromium + WebKit browser engines
steps.why: The agent lives in the project root; the test-execution layer lives in a sibling `Playwright` dir with its own deps. `npx playwright install` fetches the engines the tests run in — Chromium for the Android profile, WebKit for iOS — not bundled with the npm package.
steps.firstRun: Downloads deps plus the browser engines — the slow part (5-10 min).
steps.rerun: No-op once installed, unless a dependency or browser version changed.

steps.label: Set the target URL.
steps.why: `APP_URL` is the live app the tests open on each device profile. Unset, they fall back to a built-in default that won't be your app.

steps.label: Run it.
steps.why: The full run: executes the existing suite against the Android (`mobile-chrome`) and iOS (`mobile-safari`) profiles with step-level recording, then writes the scoreboard. `--word` additionally emits a `.docx`.
steps.firstRun: Runs every test against both device profiles from scratch.
steps.rerun: `--device android` or `--device ios` scopes to one profile; `--test-file <path>` re-runs a single test while chasing one failure.

steps.label: Open the generated report.
steps.why: The `.md` holds the per-device pass/fail scoreboard and, under each failure, numbered manual-repro steps plus a device simulator deep link.

inputs.name: APP_URL (environment variable)
inputs.desc: URL of the running app the tests open.

inputs.name: --device android | ios | all
inputs.desc: Device profile(s) to run against; defaults to both.

inputs.name: --test-file <path>, --simulator <provider>, --headed, --include-passed, --word
inputs.desc: Flags to scope to one test file, pick the simulator provider to link to, run headed, include passing tests in the report, or emit a `.docx`.

outputs.name: mobile-report-<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: Machine-readable and rendered pass/fail scoreboard, with numbered manual-repro steps under every failure.

outputs.name: mobile-report-<timestamp>.docx (optional)
outputs.desc: `.docx` of the same report; emitted only with `--word`.

outputs.name: step-results-latest.json
outputs.desc: The step-level record written during the run — the source the agent parses to pin exactly which step broke.

runbook.rerun: `--device android` or `--device ios` scopes the run to the profile you're chasing a fix on — far faster than a both-profiles run. Every run is a fresh execution; no fingerprinting here, since app behavior (not documents) is what's being exercised.
runbook.integrate: Add the `--device all` run to CI on every pull request; treat a check that fails on one profile but passes on the other as a platform-specific bug, not a flake.

video.caption: 3-min screen recording: watch the agent run the suite against two device profiles and turn one failure into numbered repro steps.
script: Open a terminal beside the app so viewers can see it in the background.
Say: 'This agent runs the app's tests on a pretend iPhone and a pretend Android, and when one fails, it hands you exact steps to see it happen yourself.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; say one line about what Node is.
Run `npm install` in the project root and in the Playwright folder (or note it's already done); mention `npx playwright install` downloads the actual browser engines it drives.
Show the one `export APP_URL=...` line; say 'this is the only place the app's address lives.'
Run `npm run mobile:test -- --word`; narrate as it runs through the Android profile, then the iPhone profile.
Open the produced `.md` report; point at the pass/fail scoreboard for each phone.
Scroll to a failure; read the numbered reproduction recipe and click the online-simulator link it generated.
Point out the plain-language recommendation at the bottom, e.g. 'failures are iPhone-only.'
Close: 'A failure nobody can reproduce gets ignored — one with numbered steps gets fixed.'
